raw_response:
I’ve been farming these 3 mu for 30 years. I never went to school, but I know my land, and I watch what my neighbors do. Two mu I do wheat then maize, same as most people around here. The other mu is cotton — I need the cash from cotton to buy things we can’t grow.

Right now it’s April, and my wheat went in last October around the 10th. I already gave it water after the winter and put urea on it when it turned green in March. Now the wheat is getting tall, so I’m watering it again and putting more urea — about half a big bag per mu. I’ll water it one more time before June if the weather stays dry. I use the seed I saved from two years ago; no point buying new seed when mine grows fine. For fertilizer, last autumn I hired the Zhang family’s small tractor to plow, and I put some of that phosphate fertilizer in the ground before planting. I don’t know kilograms — I use the big plastic scoop, about one scoop per mu. Then urea twice in spring.

After we cut the wheat in early June, I have to get the maize in fast, sometimes the same day. There’s no time to plow — I just poke holes in the stubble and drop the seeds in by hand. I put some phosphate fertilizer in each hole and cover it. If the summer is dry I’ll water it at planting and again when it’s tasseling. Last year my maize got about 800 jin per mu, so about the same this year if the weather holds.

My cotton I’m planting now in late April. I dug the furrows by hand with a hoe, dropped the seeds in, and put fertilizer in the furrow. Cotton needs picking again and again, so it takes a lot of my time in autumn, but my daughter helps when she’s home from the factory. I spray for worms if I see them — last year they were bad on Old Wang’s field, so I keep a close watch.

I don’t hire people if I can help it. My husband and eldest son work in the city now, so it’s mostly me and my mother-in-law doing the work. We only hire a small combine for the wheat harvest on two mu because it’s too much to cut by hand. Money is always tight. I heard urea went up again at the shop, so I’m being careful — maybe a little less than last year, but not too little or I’ll lose yield. Better safe than sorry. I’d rather waste a bit of fertilizer than have a bad year with no food.
